chapter: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
title: A 1934 news story of musicians suing a dance promoter
summary: Willard and Collette read a Hollywood Filmograph story about Elmer Fain's band suing for pay with the union head Mr. Johnson; Howard knows nothing of it.

bands.name: Elmer Fain and his Musical Bees

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: It's a story on the front page. You said this paper, the California News, was published by Mr. Bass, --
Yes.
Who was the husband of Charlotta Bass, who later was the publisher of the California Eagle.
Uh-huh.

On the front page is a story that says Dance Promoters Face Local Musicians. Down here -- Face Local Musicians Who Sue For Pay. Are there any musicians in here who's names you would recognize, do you suppose?
Let's see,
It says Mr. Johnson, head of the local musicians union. What Mr. Johnson --
He was president at that time.
What was Mr. Johnson's first name, does it say?
Ask Paul, he knows.
Okay, we'll ask him in a minute when we get back to -- it mentioned Elmer Fain and his Musical Bees.
Let's see, this paper was -- this was a '34 issue.
Oh, what paper is it?
It's the Hollywood Filmograph, is that what it's called?
Yes, uh-huh.
Looks about like -- it's the format of Variety. It's called the Hollywood Filmograph, March 10, 1934, with Errol Flynn on the front page.
[Pause]
Turn this off while you look.

Buddy, on the front page here, this might be something interesting for you to discuss with Mr. Howard, the story about the musicians' suit, in the union. It mentions Mr. Johnson, the head of the union, it mentions Elmer Fain and his Musical Bees. This is his mike, where's yours?
Where did this come from?
(Inaudible) that was a whole separate deal. But here's something that you may be able to help us
on. Dance Promoters Face Local Musicians Who Sue For Pay.

Now, some of these days, an overworked public may rise up to swat those who have for so long, misused it. Last Thursday, (unintelligible) dances was pulled at this Holloween, another one of the frequent high-pressure shrine out of turn. It was (unintelligible) advertised and created as a charity dance. Cash prizes for the best costume were advertised as a lure to get people in and swell the box office receipt.

Mr. Johnson, head of the local musicians union informed a news reporter yesterday, Friday, that he had filed with the public defender in the interest of Elmer Fain and his Musical Bees a claim for salaries owed to them for playing for the dance.

The musicians contend they were not paid. The names of Chauncy Hylen and George Henderson appeared on the citation slips, a defendant. According to Mrs. Mabel Gray, president of Five and Over Charity Club, the organization advertised as a charity beneficiary that at press time had not received one penny from the promoters.
No officials of the Businessmen's Social Club, advertised promoter of the dance, could be located for a statement.
Do you know anything about that? This Mr. Fain and the Musical Bees, who didn't get their money at the time.
I don't know nothing about it.
Hm?
I don't know nothing about it. But there are a lot of things I wouldn't know about.
